=== CALL C0261 ===
Gary: So, er, we just talk then, is it?
Liam: Yeah, think so. Three minutes.
Gary: Right. Where are you, then?
Liam: Normanton. Near Wakefield.
Gary: Yorkshire. I'm Dagenham. East London.
Liam: Yeah.
Gary: What d'you do?
Liam: Warehouse. Picking, like. Part-time, mostly lates, at a distribution centre off the M62. I'm knackered to be honest, did one last night and the heating's broke again, so you're freezing for eight hours.
Gary: I did warehouse when I was a kid. YTS. Didn't stick it.
Liam: Ha. It's alright. Pays for my stuff, do you know what I mean. You?
Gary: Office at a skip firm in Rainham. Phones, booking skips in, chasing people what ain't paid. My back went so they stuck me indoors. Can't complain. Well, I can. I do.
Liam: Sounds alright, that. Kettle on all day.
Gary: Kettle's the best bit of the job, mate.
Liam: Yeah.
Gary: You do a lot of these, then? Studies and that.
Liam: Yeah, loads. Surveys, cashback apps, all sorts. Do you know when this one pays out, actually?
Gary: No idea. Tracey reckons I'm addicted to 'em. The surveys.
Liam: I do trainers as well. Vinted, eBay. Sold a pair of Jordans last week for double what I paid. You just sort of look for people who don't know what they've got, like they've listed it wrong or the photos are rubbish, and you get in quick before anyone else does. Do you know what I mean.
Gary: Marketplace, me. Tools, mostly. Had a bloke last week try and mug me off on a drill, wanted forty quid for something half knackered. Got him down to fifteen.
Liam: Nice. Haggling's half of it.
Gary: Half of it. Other half's not getting done over yourself.
Liam: Yeah.
Gary: That a rugby scarf behind you?
Liam: Trinity. Wakefield Trinity, rugby league. They were rubbish at the weekend, so.
Gary: West Ham. Don't get me started. Gave my season ticket up when they moved to that soulless bowl. Watch it on the laptop now.
Liam: I'm not really fussed about football unless I've got an accumulator on. Lost it on the last game, as per.
Gary: Always the last game. I do the odd one Saturday. Scratchcards. Never win nothing.
Liam: Little laugh. Yeah.
Gary: My son's called Liam, funny enough. Twenty-six. Moved out to Romford with his girlfriend.
Liam: Yeah? I'm still at my mum's, so. Thirty and in the box room.
Gary: Nothing wrong with that. Rents round mine are a joke. Can't get a flat for under a grand.
Liam: Same up here, sort of. Not that bad, but still.
Gary: He don't ring much, mine. Once they're gone, they're gone.
Liam: Yeah, I should prob ring my dad more, to be fair, he's only in Ponte, I just—

=== CALL C0262 ===
Ryan: Hiya! Can you hear me alright? Sorry, that noise is Duke, the dog. He's snoring. If you hear something like a tractor, that's him.
Tomasz: Yes, I hear you. Hello.
Ryan: I'm Ryan. I'm in Long Eaton, sort of between Derby and Nottingham. I teach history, Head of Year 9. Still got the lanyard on, look, I've not even got changed.
Tomasz: Tomasz. Peterborough. I am electrician in a food factory, team leader for engineering on shifts.
Ryan: Oh nice, proper job that. What, keeping all the lines running?
Tomasz: Yes. Conveyors, motors, everything. New line keeps tripping out. They bring the installer, he doesn't know. I find the fault myself in one hour. Was earth leakage, cable damaged in the tray. And production manager asks every ten minutes "when is it fixed", like this helps.
Ryan: Ha! That's SLT all over. "Can you just quickly..." Do you know what I mean?
Tomasz: SLT?
Ryan: Sorry, senior leadership. Managers, basically.
Tomasz: Ah. Same everywhere.
Ryan: I noticed in your photo there's a crucifix on the wall. Do you go to church at all?
Tomasz: Why you ask this?
Ryan: Sorry, no, I wasn't being nosy. I just go myself, St Laurence's in Long Eaton. Sorry, ignore me.
Tomasz: Is okay. I am Polish, so Catholic. Christmas, Easter, and when my wife says. More culture than, you know.
Ryan: Yeah, no, I get that.
Tomasz: You go every week?
Ryan: Once a month, maybe. More when things are hard. It got me through when my dad died, to be honest. Sorry, that's a bit heavy for three minutes.
Tomasz: Is fine. You watch football?
Ryan: Oh, don't. Derby County, my whole life. My dad took me, and now I share a season ticket with my cousin. We lost again Saturday, absolutely shocking, I were mardy all Sunday. Hannah, my wife, won't let me talk about it at tea anymore.
Tomasz: Derby. This is Championship, no?
Ryan: Ha, that's harsh! Fair, but harsh.
Tomasz: My team is Lech Poznań. Also suffering. So I understand.
Ryan: Also suffering. That's going on a T-shirt. Have you got kids?
Tomasz: Two. Daughter seventeen, doing A-levels. She wants driving lessons now, thirty-five pound an hour. Is a rip-off. I can teach her in car park.
Ryan: Ha, my dad tried that with me in the Asda car park. Never again. We both came home not speaking.
Tomasz: My son is twenty, at Trent, in Nottingham.
Ryan: Oh, Nottingham, that's my patch! I did my PGCE at the uni, and the school's just on the west side. What's he studying?
Tomasz: Engineering. Mechanical. He will be proper engineer, with a degree, not like—
Ryan: Oh, that's brilliant, you must be dead proud of him, my mum still tells people I went to—

=== CALL C0263 ===
Ryan: Hiya! Sorry, give me a sec, the dog's just shifted onto my foot. Right. I'm Ryan, I'm in Long Eaton, I teach history. How you doing?
Liam: Alright. Liam. Normanton, near Wakefield.
Ryan: Oh, Wakefield! I took a school trip to the Hepworth once, lovely building, kids moaned the whole way. Is that a Trinity scarf behind you?
Liam: Yeah.
Ryan: Rugby league. I'll be honest, I know nothing about it, beyond the odd Challenge Cup final on the telly. Are they doing alright?
Liam: Not really. Rubbish at the weekend.
Ryan: Ha, join the club. Derby County, me. Lost again Saturday. I think I support them out of guilt at this point, you know, my dad got me into it and now I can't get out.
Liam: Yeah. My grandad's like that with Trinity. Tells you about players from like the sixties, every Sunday, same stories.
Ryan: Oh, I'd love that. That's basically primary sources, that, I'd be writing it all down. Sorry, history teacher. What do you do, Liam?
Liam: Warehouse. Picking, off the M62. Part-time, mostly lates.
Ryan: Oh, right! My dad were a forklift driver at a warehouse off the M1. Twenty-odd years.
Liam: Yeah? I had my counterbalance ticket. Work paid for it. It's lapsed now though. Keep meaning to redo it 'cause it pays a bit more.
Ryan: You should, honestly. Sorry, I sound like I'm talking to a Year 11. But you should.
Liam: Ha. Yeah. Prob will.
Ryan: I'm a hypocrite anyway, I've got a qualification I've half finished for about two years. Are them boxes behind you trainers?
Liam: Yeah, I resell 'em. Vinted, eBay. You look for stuff that's listed wrong, or the photos are rubbish, or someone just wants it gone quick, and you get in first. Then you clean 'em up, take decent photos, stick 'em back on for proper money. Sold some Jordans last week for double what I paid. Do you know what I mean, it adds up.
Ryan: That's actually dead clever. That's a skill, that. Most people'd just see a pair of shoes. I wouldn't have a clue. Hannah, my wife, says I dress like a geography teacher, which is an insult I've never recovered from.
Liam: Ha.
Ryan: Is that a controller on the bed as well? What do you play?
Liam: EA FC mostly. Call of Duty. With a couple of mates on headsets.
Ryan: No way, I play FC with my old uni mates! I'm awful, mind. I just sort of run at people and hope. We've got a group chat that's basically them laughing at my defending.
Liam: Yeah, most people just sprint. You've got to hold it up a bit.
Ryan: Hold it up a bit. See, that's the advice I need. Do you do it for money, the trainers, like proper side income?
Liam: Trying to. If it made enough I'd drop some hours. Maybe get a flat. I'm at my mum's still, so.
Ryan: Nothing wrong with that, mate. Me and Hannah only bought ours in 2019, I were renting a box room till I were about twenty-eight. My mum still pops round every Sunday anyway, so it's like I never left.
Liam: Yeah. Mine does a roast Sundays. That's the best bit.
Ryan: Oh, a proper Sunday roast, can't beat it. Hannah's on lates this week so it's beans on toast for my tea every night, honestly, it's grim.
Liam: Beans on toast is about my limit, to be fair.
Ryan: Ha! Well that's two of us then. Do you know when they pay out for this, by the way? I've never done one before.
Liam: No idea. I asked the other fella. He didn't know either. Hopefully before—

Gary: One eighty? Good effort. I'm on Marketplace all the time, me. Tools mostly. Bloke tried to mug me off on a drill last week, forty quid for a knackered one. I said fifteen or I walk. He took fifteen.
Tomasz: Is the only way. If you look like you want it, you pay too much.
Gary: That's it exactly. You do much on the side? Cash jobs, like?
Tomasz: Why you ask this?
Gary: Just asking, mate. Not the taxman.
Tomasz: Okay. Weekends, sometimes. Consumer unit, rewire, small things. Honestly, people doing only house jobs earn more than me. I think about it. Self-employed.
Gary: Do it. I would if I had a trade. I've got nothing. Never had a proper job for life like my old man. Ford, Dagenham, thirty years.
Tomasz: Ford. Is still there?
Gary: Engines, bits. Not like it was. Whole area's changed.
Tomasz: Everywhere is changed. I came in 2005. Wisbech, packhouse, agency. Now I am team leader. So.
Gary: Twenty years? You're basically from here then.
Tomasz: No. I am Polish who lives here. My kids, yes, they are English. They talk like you.
Gary: Ha, God help 'em. You into football?
Tomasz: Premier League. Polish national team. You are West Ham, I think? I saw in the photo, the cushion.
Gary: West Ham, yeah. Gave the season ticket up when they moved to that soulless bowl. Watch it on the laptop now, on a dodgy stream.
Tomasz: Soulless bowl. I will use this. My son says same about—
calls.C0265:
Tomasz: Hello. Tomasz, Peterborough.
Liam: Alright. Liam. Normanton, near Wakefield.
Tomasz: Wakefield. Okay.
Liam: Yeah.
Tomasz: You work?
Liam: Warehouse. Picking. Part-time, four shifts, mostly lates.
Tomasz: Part-time. Why part-time? You are young.
Liam: Leaves my days free, like. I do trainers on the side, reselling. And I'm knackered enough on four, to be honest.
Tomasz: Four shifts and knackered. I do forty hours, rotating, early and late. Last night I did night shift. Is normal.
Liam: Little laugh. Yeah, fair enough. What d'you do?
Tomasz: Electrician in a food factory. Team leader. If a line stops, they call me.
Liam: We've got engineers like that at ours. Everyone goes quiet when they walk past.
Tomasz: Good. They should go quiet.
Liam: Ha. Yeah.
Tomasz: You drive forklift?
Liam: I had the ticket, counterbalance. Work paid. It's lapsed now, though. Keep meaning to book it again, 'cause it's a bit more an hour.
Tomasz: So book it. Is one phone call.
Liam: Yeah. Prob will. Everyone keeps saying that today.
Tomasz: Then everyone is right, no?
Liam: Yeah, suppose.
Tomasz: What car you have?
Liam: Old Golf. Mk6. Keep it clean, mind, it's mint inside. Needs an MOT though, and I'm skint till Friday, so I'm sort of hoping nothing comes up on it.
Tomasz: What year?
Liam: 2010. Done about a hundred and twenty thousand.
Tomasz: Check the suspension, the front, the drop links. On Golf this age they always knock. And the brake discs. If you do yourself before MOT, you save a lot. Garage will charge you double for parts and labour, they see young guy, they see money.
Liam: I can do bulbs and that. Fluids. Never done discs.
Tomasz: Is not difficult. YouTube, a jack, two hours. My son did his first one at sixteen with me.
Liam: Yeah? I did start a mechanics course at college. Level 2. Packed it in after about six months.
Tomasz: Why?
Liam: Dunno. Didn't fancy it at the time. Wish I'd stuck at it now, to be fair, 'cause I'd be on decent money.
Tomasz: Is not too late. Thirty?
Liam: Thirty, yeah.
Tomasz: I am forty-eight, I did inspection and testing course at college here, Peterborough, three years ago. In English, which is not my language. You can do level 2 at thirty.
Liam: Yeah. Maybe. What d'you drive, then?
Tomasz: BMW, Five Series. Old one. I just got the alloys off Facebook, he wanted three hundred, I paid one eighty.
Liam: Nice. That's how I do trainers. Never pay what they ask. If you look keen, you're done.
Tomasz: Exactly this. If you look like you want it, you pay too much. Same with cars, same with everything.
Liam: Do you know what I mean. People just click buy.
Tomasz: My daughter is like this. Everything is click, click, it arrives. She wants driving lessons now, thirty-five pound an hour, I say—
calls.C0266:
Ryan: Hiya! Gary, is it? I'm Ryan. Long Eaton, between Derby and Nottingham. How you doing?
Gary: Alright. Dagenham.
Ryan: Dagenham, brilliant. Is that a West Ham cushion I saw in your photo?
Gary: Yeah.
Ryan: I'm Derby, so I'm not in a position to laugh at anyone. We lost again Saturday. I think I'm just a glutton for punishment at this point.
Gary: At least you've got a proper ground. We got moved to that soulless bowl. Gave up my season ticket over it. Thirty-odd years at Upton Park, then they stick you in a running track with a roof.
Ryan: Oh, that's grim. Upton Park was a proper ground, though. My dad took me there once, actually, we lost two-nil and he still said it was one of the best atmospheres he'd been in.
Gary: It was. Gone now. Flats.
Ryan: Flats. Course it is. Sorry, I'm a history teacher, so I get really sad about that sort of thing. Old grounds, old factories.
Gary: Thought you was a teacher.
Ryan: Is it the lanyard? It's always the lanyard. What do you do, Gary?
Gary: Office at a skip firm. Rainham. Phones, booking skips, chasing money.
Ryan: Chasing money. I bet you're good at that.
Gary: I don't let 'em off, put it that way. They say the cheque's in the post, I ring every day till it is.
Ryan: Ha! I should get you to chase my Year 9 homework. Half of them have owed me an essay since September.
Gary: Same thing really. Just younger.
Ryan: Just younger, ha! Was that your son in the graduation photo behind you?
Gary: Yeah. Liam. Did a course at college, business or summat. Moved to Romford with his girlfriend.
Ryan: Aw, you must be proud of him. Do you see much of him?
Gary: Not really. He's busy. That's how it goes.
Ryan: Yeah. My mum says the same about me, and I'm ten minutes away. I still feel guilty. Sorry, I'm rambling. Do you do anything outside work?
Gary: Not much. Surveys. These. Pub quiz now and then if the wife drags me.
Ryan: Oh, pub quiz! I do one every week, I'm the history and sport man. We came second last week by one point. One point, Gary. It was a question on the Tudors and I got it wrong. I'm meant to be the Tudors man.
Gary: I'm the telly one. Quiz shows, Only Fools. Can't do the music round.
Ryan: Nobody can do the music round. It's always some band from 1983 nobody's heard of.
Gary: Pays out on the meat raffle, ours. That's the only reason I go.
Ryan: Ha, a meat raffle! Now that's a proper prize. What did you win?
Gary: Leg of lamb once. Tracey done it for Sunday dinner. Best thing I ever won.
Ryan: Best thing he ever won. A leg of lamb. Honestly, that's lovely. My dad won a—

C0263.line_text: Ryan: That's actually dead clever. That's a skill, that. Most people'd just see a pair of shoes. I wouldn't have a clue. Hannah, my wife, says I dress like a geography teacher, which is an insult I've never recovered from.
C0263.what: While Ryan is talking, Liam's eyes drop below the camera to his lap three or four times, and the bluish light on his face brightens briefly as if a phone screen has lit up. He looks back up at the screen each time after a second or two.
